title: Scarcity and economising
context: Analyze scarcity, economising, and who participates in economic decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity disappears once a household earns a steady salary because income removes all limits.
Economising means making careful use of limited resources rather than treating them as if they were unlimited.
Nobody can fully opt out of economic decisions, because even inaction is a choice about scarce time or money.
Only registered businesses face scarcity; households with regular income never need to economise on their spending.
Exchange requires that at least one party is an entrepreneur; households can never participate directly in exchange.
tactical_explanations:
Steady salary does not switch scarcity off. A household with regular pay still faces a finite monthly budget and finite hours in the day — rent, food, transport, and leisure compete for the same euros. Income changes which constraint bites hardest; it does not remove the fact that wants exceed what the paycheck can cover.

Picture a nurse who earns a reliable wage yet still chooses between a weekend trip and repairing the washing machine. That choice only exists because scarcity survived the salary. The claim that income removes all limits confuses “more room to choose” with “no limits left.”

So the statement is False.

Economising is careful use of limited resources, not treating them as endless.

So the statement is True.

Skipping a purchase is still a decision about scarce time or money. Sitting on the sofa instead of shopping does not eject you from economic life; it ranks “do nothing now” above other uses of those hours and euros. Nobody gets a clean exit simply by inactivity.

So the statement is True.

Registered firms are not the only ones who meet limits. A family with steady income still rations rent, groceries, and leisure against a finite budget each month. Treating scarcity as a business-only problem ignores ordinary household economising — the weekly shop, the heating bill, the decision to repair rather than replace.

So the statement is False.

Households trade every day: buying bread, paying for a haircut, selling a used bike. Entrepreneur status is not a ticket of admission to exchange.

So the statement is False.

title: Goods, services, needs, and wants
context: Analyze the distinction between goods, services, needs, and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Goods must be intangible; any tangible item automatically counts as a service instead.
Services are intangible activities performed for someone, such as installing software or preparing a drink.
Needs are things necessary for well-being, whereas wants are desired but not essential for basic well-being.
Both households and businesses have needs that may be fulfilled through exchange with other economic actors.
Scarcity means resources are limited, so individuals and businesses must economise rather than assume unlimited supply.
tactical_explanations:
Goods are tangible items such as a loaf or a coat, not intangible activities.

So the statement is False.

A service is work done for someone without handing over a lasting object: installing software or preparing a drink fits that test. The intangibility of the activity is what places it on the service side of the goods–services line.

So the statement is True.

Needs keep basic well-being going — food, shelter, essential care — while wants are desired extras that are not required for that baseline. The statement’s split matches how the chapter separates what you must cover from what you merely desire.

A household can skip a cinema night and still be okay; skipping food or heat is a different category. That contrast is exactly the needs-versus-wants distinction, and it survives even when both are bought in the same weekly shop.

So the statement is True.

Families need food and shelter; firms need staff, materials, and working equipment. Either side can meet those needs by trading with the other — groceries for cash, wages for labour, parts for invoices.

So the statement is True.

Limited resources force careful choices: that is scarcity, and economising is the response. Assuming unlimited supply would ignore the constraint the chapter starts from.

So the statement is True.

title: Households, entrepreneurs, and everyday exchange
context: Analyze the roles of households and entrepreneurs in everyday exchange of goods and services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Only consumers ever exchange goods; businesses are legally barred from all trade with households.
Only individual consumers have needs; registered businesses operate with zero internal needs of their own.
Choosing to keep pocket money unspent means a teenager has avoided making any economic decision.
Exchange is one way needs and wants get fulfilled when households and businesses trade with each other.
Because money is used, barter arrangements can never count as genuine exchange.
tactical_explanations:
Businesses trade with households every day — selling goods, buying labour, hiring suppliers. There is no legal bar that confines exchange to consumers alone.

A bakery sells loaves to families; a café buys milk from a dairy; a teenager sells a used console online. Trade runs both ways across the household–firm boundary, not only from shoppers toward empty shelves.

So the statement is False.

Shops need stock, premises, and staff — businesses are not need-free.

So the statement is False.

Leaving pocket money unspent is still a choice about scarce cash — save now, spend later, or hold it. The teenager has not stepped outside economic decision-making by refusing to buy.

So the statement is False.

When a household pays a firm for something useful, exchange fulfils a need or want through trade.

So the statement is True.

Barter is exchange without money: gardening help for a bookshelf still swaps valued things. Cash is common, not required for the swap to count as genuine exchange.

Imagine two neighbours agreeing that one mows the lawn while the other builds a shelf. No euros change hands, yet each gives something the other values — that is exchange under another payment form, not a non-economic favour outside the chapter’s map.

So the statement is False.

title: Business Operations and Institutional Needs
context: Consider households, startups, and manufacturing firms interacting in a market system. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses provide goods like computers and services like installing software for people to satisfy their needs.
Manufacturers of smartphones may have an operational need for electronic components produced by specialised suppliers.
To fabricate components, a manufacturer requires raw materials and a workforce rather than operating in isolation.
Individuals frequently exchange goods and services directly and are fully active participants in trading.
Households need food, shelter, and medical care, and they also want leisure activities such as cinema visits.
tactical_explanations:
Computers are goods; installing software is a service — both help people meet needs.

So the statement is True.

A smartphone maker cannot assemble handsets without specialised electronic parts from suppliers. That input requirement is an operational need of the manufacturer, not a consumer-side curiosity. Without those components, the production line stops regardless of how strong final demand looks.

So the statement is True.

Fabricating components means drawing on raw materials and a workforce; isolation is not how production works. A plant that tried to invent every input alone would still need people and materials from somewhere.

So the statement is True.

People buy, sell, and swap goods and services directly — they are full participants in trade, not spectators standing outside the market while firms alone move resources.

So the statement is True.

Food, shelter, and medical care are household needs; cinema nights are wants layered on top. Both sit inside everyday household demand, but only the first group is essential for basic well-being.

A family that skips the film is still housed and fed; a family that cannot cover rent faces a different problem. Keeping that split clear matters when you classify why households enter exchange.

So the statement is True.

title: Corner café: beans and cappuccinos
context: Consider a corner café where customers buy bags of coffee beans and pay baristas to prepare drinks. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bag of roasted beans is a good and the barista's drink preparation is a service.
Needs and wants are identical concepts, so there is no meaningful difference between craving caffeine and a flavoured latte.
A habitual craving for a particular drink is more accurately a want if it is not essential for basic well-being.
Because the café is a business, it cannot itself be said to have needs such as reliable suppliers.
Paying for beans or drinks fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides of the transaction.
tactical_explanations:
Roasted beans are a good; barista drink preparation is a service.

So the statement is True.

Needing enough caffeine to function is not the same as craving a flavoured latte for pleasure. Needs cover basic well-being; wants cover non-essential desires — the concepts are not identical, even when both involve coffee.

A customer who buys plain filter coffee to stay awake for a night shift is closer to a functional need than one who orders a caramel-syrup cappuccino purely for taste. Collapsing both into one label erases that difference and misreads the café counter.

So the statement is False.

A habitual craving for a particular drink is more accurately a want when it is not essential for basic well-being. Enjoyment and habit do not automatically turn the order into a need.

So the statement is True.

Cafés need reliable bean suppliers, working machines, and staff just as any other firm needs inputs. Being a business does not erase those operational needs — without beans or a working grinder, the menu stops.

So the statement is False.

Paying for beans or drinks is exchange: the customer gets a good or service, the café gets revenue that can meet its own bills.

So the statement is True.

title: Jonas: bus pass or game skin
context: Consider jonas has twelve euros pocket money and must choose between an eight-euro bus pass and a ten-euro game skin. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bus pass is a need for getting to school, while the game skin is a want rather than a basic necessity.
Because both items have a price, they must both be classified as needs rather than wants.
Individuals face economic decisions about scarce resources even before they run a business or register as entrepreneurs.
Choosing to save the twelve euros and buy nothing means Jonas has opted out of all economic decision-making.
Once Jonas buys the bus pass, his want for the game skin permanently disappears and can never return.
tactical_explanations:
The bus pass is a school-travel need; the game skin is a non-essential want.

So the statement is True.

A price on both items does not turn the game skin into a need. Needs and wants can both cost money; classification follows well-being, not the sticker.

Jonas could skip the skin and still reach school with a pass. Treating every priced item as a need would erase the chapter’s distinction the moment a shop attaches a euro amount to cosmetics and transport alike.

So the statement is False.

Scarce time and pocket money force choices long before anyone registers a firm. Individuals face economic decisions as soon as resources are limited relative to competing uses — school transport versus game cosmetics included.

So the statement is False.

Saving the twelve euros and buying nothing is still a ranking of scarce cash: hold it, spend later, or spend now. Jonas has not opted out of economic decision-making by refusing the purchase.

So the statement is False.

Buying the bus pass does not delete the want for the game skin forever. Wants can return next month when pocket money refreshes; satisfying one claim on the budget does not erase other desires.

Picture Jonas riding to school with the pass and still browsing the skin shop on his phone. The want survived the purchase. Permanent disappearance is not how wants behave after a single alternative spend.

So the statement is False.

title: PhoneFix screen repairs
context: Consider phoneFix Wien replaces cracked screens using spare parts ordered in limited monthly batches. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Screen replacement is a service, while a phone case sold at the counter is a good.
Because PhoneFix is a business rather than a household, its monthly spare parts can never run scarce.
A customer buying a decorative case purely for its design is satisfying a want rather than a basic need.
Repairing a phone never fulfils a need because phones are luxury items outside normal economic analysis.
A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise by prioritising which jobs to accept.
tactical_explanations:
Screen replacement is a service; a phone case on the shelf is a good.

So the statement is True.

PhoneFix still faces scarce spare parts each month even though it is a business. Firm status does not invent unlimited inventory; a thin batch of screens forces triage of which repairs to take.

A shop that burns through its monthly allotment by Wednesday cannot magic more modules into existence because it has a trade licence. Scarcity of parts is an operational fact, not a household-only problem.

So the statement is False.

A decorative case bought purely for design satisfies a want, not a basic need. Style preference does not become essential well-being just because the item protects a phone.

So the statement is True.

Phones can be central to work and contact; repairing one can fulfil a genuine need. Calling every handset a luxury outside economics misreads how households use communication devices day to day.

So the statement is False.

A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise: prioritise urgent jobs, defer others, or refuse overflow. That allocation under a hard stock cap is textbook economising.

So the statement is True.

title: Defining the economy from scratch
context: Consider during a first lesson students list core building blocks of economic life. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The economy consists essentially of households and entrepreneurs interacting with one another.
Goods are tangible items, whereas services are intangible activities performed for someone.
Both households and businesses have needs, and exchange is one way those needs and wants get fulfilled.
Scarcity forces individuals and businesses to economise rather than assume unlimited resources.
Nobody, whether a household or a business, can truly opt out of making economic decisions.
tactical_explanations:
Households and entrepreneurs interacting form the economy’s core cast.

So the statement is True.

Goods are tangible items you can hold; services are intangible activities performed for someone. A loaf versus a haircut is the standard illustration of that split.

So the statement is True.

Both households and businesses have needs — food and shelter on one side, stock and staff on the other — and exchange is one way those needs and wants get fulfilled when the two sides trade.

A family pays a bakery for bread; the bakery pays a miller for flour. Needs travel through those swaps rather than vanishing because one party is a firm.

So the statement is True.

Scarcity means resources are limited relative to competing uses, so individuals and businesses must economise instead of assuming unlimited supply. Careful allocation is the rational response to that constraint.

Ignoring the limit — spending as if time, money, and materials never run out — is exactly what economising rejects. The statement states that discipline correctly.

So the statement is True.

Nobody truly opts out: even “doing nothing” ranks scarce time or money against other options. Households and businesses alike stay inside economic decision-making.

So the statement is True.

title: Herr Novak's bakery
context: Consider herr Novak sells bread at his Linz bakery and charges one euro extra for doorstep delivery. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Herr Novak acts as an entrepreneur, while the families buying his bread act as households.
Bread is a good and doorstep delivery is a service, matching the distinction between tangible and intangible offerings.
Because Herr Novak owns a business, he personally has no needs of his own.
Paying for delivery is not exchange because a service has no monetary value once it has been performed.
Flour and oven fuel are unlimited for any bakery, so Herr Novak never has to economise on ingredients.
tactical_explanations:
Herr Novak is the entrepreneur; bread-buying families are households.

So the statement is True.

Bread is a tangible good; doorstep delivery is an intangible service. The bakery can sell both in one order without collapsing the distinction.

So the statement is True.

Owning a business does not erase personal needs. Herr Novak still needs food, rest, and income for his own household life even while he runs the bakery. Entrepreneur status and personal needs coexist.

A baker who works sixteen-hour days still has to eat and sleep. Treating the owner as a need-free machine confuses the firm’s role with the person’s biology and budget.

So the statement is False.

Paying for delivery is still exchange: money for a service that has value when performed. Finished work does not erase that it was traded.

So the statement is False.

Flour and oven fuel are limited inputs. Any bakery that treats them as unlimited will over-order, waste heat, or run out mid-bake — so Herr Novak must economise on ingredients like every other producer.

So the statement is False.

title: Exchange without money
context: Assess statements about exchange, barter, and fulfilling needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Two neighbours swapping gardening lessons for a handmade bookshelf still counts as exchange even without money.
Exchange can only occur when euro banknotes or electronic transfers are used between the parties.
Wood used to build the bookshelf is a limited resource, so the carpenter must economise on how much he uses.
Gardening lessons are a service because they are an activity performed for the neighbour, not a physical item.
Individuals, not only businesses, have needs and wants that direct exchange can help satisfy.
tactical_explanations:
Gardening lessons swapped for a bookshelf still count as exchange without money.

So the statement is True.

Exchange does not require euro banknotes or electronic transfers. Barter — lessons for a bookshelf — is exchange under another payment form. Insisting on cash-only trade would erase neighbour swaps that clearly move valued goods and services.

If only bank transfers counted, those two neighbours would be “outside” exchange while each still gains something the other supplies. That is an artificial gate the chapter does not set.

So the statement is False.

Wood used to build the bookshelf is a limited resource, so the carpenter must economise on how much he uses per piece — cut carefully, avoid waste, choose dimensions that fit the available timber.

So the statement is True.

Gardening lessons are an activity performed for the neighbour — a service, not a physical object.

So the statement is True.

Individuals, not only businesses, have needs and wants that direct exchange can help satisfy — food grown, shelves built, skills shared between people without a shopfront.

So the statement is True.

title: Petra's dining table commission
context: Consider petra pays carpenter Fabian 650 euros for an oak dining table he builds and delivers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Petra's family acts as a household and Fabian acts as an entrepreneur in this transaction.
The finished dining table is a good because it is a tangible item Fabian produces and delivers.
Paying for the table fulfils the family's need for furniture through exchange.
Fabian has no genuine need for timber because raw materials are merely wants for any business.
Timber is a limited resource, so Fabian must economise on how much oak he uses per commission.
tactical_explanations:
Petra’s family is the household; Fabian is the entrepreneur in the trade.

So the statement is True.

The finished dining table is a tangible good Fabian produces and delivers to the family.

So the statement is True.

Paying for the table fulfils the family’s furniture need through exchange: money for a usable good that meets a household requirement rather than a gift or a favour outside trade.

So the statement is True.

Timber is a genuine operational need for a carpenter, not a mere want. Without oak or similar stock, Fabian cannot build the commission. Calling raw materials “only wants” mislabels a production input as optional desire.

A workshop that runs out of boards cannot deliver tables no matter how strong customer demand is. That shortage is a needs problem on the firm side, not a cosmetic preference.

So the statement is False.

Timber is limited, so Fabian must economise on oak per commission — design cuts, scrap rates, and board choice all ration the stock.

So the statement is True.

title: Needs, wants, and who has them
context: Analyze claims about needs, wants, and which actors in the economy face them. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A manufacturer of laptops may need specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production running.
High-tech manufacturers have zero internal needs because only end consumers ever experience genuine need.
Households buy goods and services from businesses to satisfy both needs and wants in daily life.
Wants disappear automatically once every need has been fully satisfied in a given month.
Teenagers with pocket money are outside the economy until they register a business or join a formal household.
tactical_explanations:
Laptop makers need specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production running.

So the statement is True.

High-tech firms have internal needs — components, skilled staff, power, premises — just as end consumers have needs. Restricting “genuine need” to shoppers alone would leave the factory unexplained when parts run short.

An assembler waiting on delayed chips is experiencing a real production need. Pretending only final buyers feel need erases that side of the economy and misreads why firms enter exchange for inputs.

So the statement is False.

Households buy goods and services from businesses to satisfy both needs and wants in daily life — groceries and heating alongside cinema tickets and gadgets.

So the statement is True.

Wants do not vanish automatically once monthly needs are covered. Extra desires can appear or persist even after rent and food are paid — new trainers, a trip, a better phone.

So the statement is False.

Teenagers with pocket money already make scarce-resource choices inside the economy. They do not wait for a business licence or formal household registration to start economising on allowance and time.

So the statement is False.

title: Lukas end-of-month pocket money
context: Consider student Lukas has 300 euros monthly for transport, toiletries, and designer trainers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Ninety euros for transport and toiletries covers needs, while 140-euro trainers cover a want.
Because Lukas receives money from parents, he is not part of the household side of the economy.
Buying trainers makes his need for transport disappear for the rest of the month.
Wanting trainers is irrational and therefore falls outside the scope of economics entirely.
A fixed monthly sum is an unlimited resource that never needs to be economised.
tactical_explanations:
Transport and toiletries are needs; the 140-euro trainers are a want.

So the statement is True.

Receiving money from parents still places Lukas on the household side of the economy. Pocket money is a household transfer, not an exit pass from economic life.

A student who budgets the allowance between bus fares and trainers is exactly the household decision-maker the chapter describes — dependent funding does not erase the role or the scarcity of the monthly sum.

So the statement is False.

Buying trainers does not cancel the need for transport for the rest of the month. Needs and wants compete for the same budget; satisfying one claim leaves the other intact.

So the statement is False.

Wanting trainers is a preference economics can analyse; “irrational” is not a reason to eject the desire from the subject. Scarce money still forces a choice whether or not outsiders approve of the purchase.

So the statement is False.

A fixed monthly sum is a limited resource that must be economised across competing uses. Calling it unlimited contradicts the hard cap of the allowance itself — once the euros are spent, nothing remains to stretch.

So the statement is False.

title: Farmer Reinisch's market stall
context: Consider farmer Reinisch sells potatoes and carrots from eight hectares at a Saturday village market. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Reinisch acts as an entrepreneur at the stall while village buyers act as households.
Because farmland can theoretically be bought elsewhere, Reinisch's eight hectares should not be treated as scarce.
Potatoes and carrots are goods rather than services even though they must be cooked before eating.
Splitting eight hectares between crops is an economic decision Reinisch cannot avoid given limited land.
Paying cash at the stall is not genuine exchange because only barter counts as real economic trade.
tactical_explanations:
Reinisch sells as an entrepreneur; village buyers act as households.

So the statement is True.

Farmland elsewhere does not make Reinisch’s eight hectares non-scarce for him. What he can plant this season is limited by the fields he controls; theoretical purchases elsewhere do not expand today’s acreage.

If he splits the eight hectares between potatoes and carrots, every extra row of one crop means fewer rows of the other. That trade-off is scarcity on his own land, regardless of listings in another district.

So the statement is False.

Potatoes and carrots are tangible goods even if cooked later; preparation does not turn them into services.

So the statement is True.

Splitting eight hectares between crops is an economic decision Reinisch cannot avoid given limited land. Allocation under a hard acreage cap is economising in plain form.

So the statement is True.

Cash at the stall is genuine exchange — money for goods. Barter is one form, not the only form that counts.

So the statement is False.

title: Market day in Hallstatt
context: Consider toni sells cheese wheels; Rosa offers children's face-painting; families buy for groceries or fun. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Toni and Rosa act as entrepreneurs while visiting families act as households.
A cheese wheel is a good and face-painting is a service.
Buying cheese for weekly groceries satisfies a need, while face-painting satisfies more of a want.
Paying for cheese or face-painting fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides.
Because Toni has only thirty wheels left, he must economise by allocating stock among queuing families.
tactical_explanations:
Toni and Rosa organise stalls and sell as entrepreneurs; visiting families buy as households. Market day puts those roles face to face.

So the statement is True.

A cheese wheel is a tangible good; face-painting is an activity performed for a child — a service.

So the statement is True.

Cheese for weekly groceries leans toward a need; face-painting for festival fun leans toward a want. Both can be bought on the same square without collapsing the categories.

So the statement is True.

Paying for cheese or face-painting is exchange on both sides: buyers get a good or service, sellers get revenue that can meet their own needs or wants.

So the statement is True.

With only thirty wheels left, Toni must allocate stock among queuing families — who gets a full wheel, who gets a half, who waits. That rationing under a hard inventory cap is economising in public view.

A seller who pretends the remaining wheels are unlimited will over-promise and leave the last customers empty-handed. Scarcity of stock forces the allocation choice whether or not Toni likes making it.

So the statement is True.

title: Scarcity across actors
context: Assess whether scarcity and economising apply uniformly. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A multinational corporation with large cash reserves still faces scarce managerial attention and factory capacity.
Households never economise because their wants are unlimited and budgets therefore do not constrain them.
Governments are excluded from scarcity because they can always raise taxes to fund any project immediately.
Economising is rational behaviour when a resource is limited relative to competing uses.
Entrepreneurs must economise on inputs such as labour hours and raw materials to stay viable.
tactical_explanations:
Cash reserves do not erase scarce managerial attention or factory capacity.

So the statement is True.

Unlimited wants do not free households from budgets. Wants being open-ended is exactly why limited income forces economising — more desires than euros.

A family that wants a holiday, new furniture, and a car still faces a paycheck that cannot fund all three at once. Pretending budgets do not constrain because wants are unlimited reverses the logic: unlimited wants make the budget bite harder.

So the statement is False.

Governments face scarce time, political capital, and real resources even when they can tax. Raising revenue does not instantly create unlimited capacity for every project on the wishlist.

So the statement is False.

Economising is rational when a resource is limited relative to competing uses — allocate carefully instead of treating the stock as endless.

So the statement is True.

Entrepreneurs must economise on labour hours and raw materials to stay viable. Input limits are everyday firm constraints, not optional thrift for “small” producers only.

So the statement is True.

title: Kaffee Ecke morning queue
context: Consider owner Sami sells bean bags and employs baristas; a rare Ethiopian lot is limited to forty kilograms. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sami supplies goods and services as an entrepreneur while customers act as households.
The bean bag is a good and espresso preparation is a service.
A strong habitual coffee craving may reflect a want rather than a strict survival need.
Trying a new seasonal flavour for enjoyment is best classified as a want.
The forty-kilogram cap forces Sami to economise on how he allocates beans across the season.
tactical_explanations:
Sami is the entrepreneur; coffee customers act as households in the queue.

So the statement is True.

The bean bag is a tangible good; espresso preparation is work performed — a service. Both can leave the same counter without merging categories into one vague “coffee product.”

So the statement is True.

A strong habitual coffee craving may still be a want rather than a strict survival need. Habit and enjoyment do not automatically equal essential well-being, even when the craving feels urgent before work.

So the statement is True.

Trying a new seasonal flavour for enjoyment is a want, not a basic well-being need.

So the statement is True.

A forty-kilogram seasonal bean cap forces Sami to allocate roast across drinks, retail bags, and days of the week. That hard weight limit is scarcity; spreading it carefully is economising.

If he pours most of the stock into one popular drink in week one, later weeks run dry. The cap makes those trade-offs unavoidable whether or not morning demand feels endless at the till.

So the statement is True.

title: Classmates swap novels for algebra help
context: Consider nora lends Felix novels; Felix tutors her two afternoons with no money exchanged. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Exchange requires money, so this novels-for-tutoring swap does not count as exchange at all.
Felix's tutoring is a service and Nora's novels are goods, matching the standard classification.
Because both are students rather than businesses, needs, wants, and exchange concepts do not apply.
Felix's limited free time is a scarce resource allocated between tutoring and his other commitments.
Once the swap is agreed, both have opted out of any further economic decisions about their time.
tactical_explanations:
Novels-for-tutoring is exchange without money: each classmate gives something the other values. Cash is not a required ingredient for the swap to count.

If only euros defined exchange, Felix’s algebra help and Nora’s books would sit outside economics while clearly moving valued services and goods between them. That cash-only gate is artificial and would mislabel an obvious trade of help for novels.

So the statement is False.

Felix’s tutoring is a service; Nora’s novels are goods under the usual split.

So the statement is True.

Students still have needs, wants, and scarce time. Being not-yet-businesses does not eject them from exchange concepts — the swap itself is economic activity between two people.

So the statement is False.

Felix’s limited free time is a scarce resource allocated between tutoring and other commitments. Agreeing to help Nora means fewer hours for something else that week.

So the statement is True.

Agreeing the swap does not end further economic decisions about remaining time.

So the statement is False.

title: Opting out of the economy?
context: Analyze whether households or businesses can successfully opt out of economic decisions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Retired couples growing their own food still face scarcity of land, time, and seed and must economise.
Repairing a customer's bicycle at a workshop is a service because it is work performed rather than an item handed over.
Selling surplus eggs to neighbours for cash is exchange that fulfils buyers' needs or wants.
Because retirees no longer earn wages, they must be classified as entrepreneurs rather than households.
Deciding how much land to plant versus how many chickens to keep is an unavoidable economic choice.
tactical_explanations:
Self-grown food still faces scarce land, time, and seed — retirees must economise.

So the statement is True.

Bicycle repair at a workshop is work performed — a service — not mainly an item handed over as the product sold.

So the statement is True.

Selling surplus eggs to neighbours for cash is exchange that can fulfil buyers’ needs or wants while giving the retirees income or trade value in return. Money changing hands for food is ordinary household–neighbour trade, not a non-economic gift just because the sellers are retired.

So the statement is True.

No longer earning wages does not reclassify retirees as entrepreneurs by default. Growing food and selling eggs can include household roles; pension status alone does not force the entrepreneur label.

A couple planting for their own kitchen is acting as a household meeting its own needs. Occasional egg sales do not automatically rewrite that primary role into “entrepreneur instead of household.”

So the statement is False.

How much land to plant versus how many chickens to keep is an unavoidable economic choice under limits.

So the statement is True.

title: Remote cabin and firewood trade
context: Consider karl lives in a remote cabin and occasionally trades firewood for canned food from hikers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The occasional firewood-for-food trade is exchange fulfilling needs even without shops nearby.
Because Karl avoids shops, he has genuinely opted out of making economic decisions.
Karl's claim that he needs nobody proves scarcity no longer applies to him personally.
Chopping firewood requires no economising because forests are unlimited resources for anyone living remotely.
Only members of registered businesses or official households are affected by needs, wants, and scarcity.
tactical_explanations:
Firewood-for-food trade fulfils needs through exchange even without nearby shops.

So the statement is True.

Avoiding shops does not mean Karl has opted out of economic decisions. He still allocates scarce time to chopping wood, storing food, and arranging trades with neighbours.

A cabin dweller who spends a morning on firewood instead of fishing has ranked scarce hours. Distance from retail does not create an exit from that kind of choice or from scarcity of energy and stores.

So the statement is False.

Claiming he needs nobody does not abolish scarcity for Karl. Land, time, tools, and energy remain limited relative to what he wants done around the cabin.

So the statement is False.

Forests are not unlimited for one person in one season. Chopping firewood still requires economising on time, dry wood access, and storage — remote living does not invent infinite timber on demand.

So the statement is False.

Needs, wants, and scarcity affect individuals whether or not they hold a business licence or sit in an “official” household form. Karl’s cabin life is still inside those constraints.

So the statement is False.

title: Electrician Boris and the Hoffmanns
context: Consider the Hoffmanns pay Boris 180 euros for kitchen wiring; that evening Boris buys groceries for his family. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The Hoffmanns act as a household paying for repair; Boris acts as an entrepreneur supplying it.
Electrical repair is a service because it is work performed rather than a physical item delivered.
Faulty wiring created a need for a working system fulfilled through exchange of money for service.
When Boris buys groceries later, he acts as a household with needs of his own.
Boris's limited working hours are a scarce resource he must economise across jobs.
tactical_explanations:
Hoffmanns pay as a household; Boris supplies the repair as an entrepreneur.

So the statement is True.

Electrical repair is work performed rather than a physical item delivered as the product — a service that restores function in the home when wiring fails. The Hoffmanns pay for skilled labour, not for a boxed appliance left on the doorstep.

So the statement is True.

Faulty wiring created a need for a working system; paying Boris fulfils that need through exchange of money for skilled service at the property.

So the statement is True.

When Boris buys groceries later, he acts as a household with needs of his own. Entrepreneur by day does not erase household roles after hours.

An electrician who invoices the Hoffmanns in the afternoon and shops for dinner in the evening switches roles without contradiction. Both sides of economic life apply to the same person at different moments, and groceries remain a household need even for someone who runs a trade.

So the statement is True.

Boris’s limited working hours are scarce and must be economised across jobs.

So the statement is True.

title: Goods versus services traps
context: Review subtle classification traps distinguishing goods from services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Installing software on a customer's computer is a service, not a good, even though it involves a physical machine.
A downloadable e-book file is a service because it has no weight and therefore cannot be a good.
Only goods, never services, can be exchanged in a market between households and firms.
A restaurant meal eaten on the premises is a good because food is always tangible.
Delivery of a pizza to a customer's door converts the pizza from a service into a good.
tactical_explanations:
Software installation is a service even when a physical computer is involved.

So the statement is True.

A downloadable e-book is still a good in the digital sense: a lasting product transferred to the buyer, not an activity performed live. Lack of weight does not automatically make it a service.

Calling every weightless file a service would turn music downloads, e-books, and software licences into “services” by mass alone, blurring the chapter’s activity-versus-item line beyond recognition.

So the statement is False.

Services are exchanged in markets every day — repairs, lessons, deliveries — alongside goods. Markets are not goods-only clubs closed to intangible activities.

So the statement is False.

A restaurant meal mixes food with preparation and service on the premises; treating it as “always only a good because food is tangible” oversimplifies what the diner pays for at the table.

So the statement is False.

Delivering a pizza does not convert the pizza from a service into a good by magic of the doorbell. The food remains a good; the delivery run is a service layered on top.

So the statement is False.

title: Street musician tips
context: Consider elena busks on the main square; listeners drop coins into her case for violin performances. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Elena's performance is a service because it is an activity enjoyed rather than a physical item handed over.
Listeners paying because they enjoy the atmosphere are satisfying a want rather than a basic survival need.
Because each tip amount is voluntary and unfixed, no exchange takes place between Elena and the listeners.
Elena's need to cover rent shows that individuals, not only registered businesses, experience economic needs.
Elena's limited performing time each Sunday is a scarce resource she must economise across locations.
tactical_explanations:
Elena’s street performance is a service — activity enjoyed, not an item handed over.

So the statement is True.

Listeners tipping for atmosphere satisfy a want, not a basic survival need. Enjoyment of music is desirable, not essential well-being.

So the statement is True.

Voluntary, unfixed tip amounts can still be exchange: listeners give money, Elena gives a performance they value. Lack of a posted price does not erase the swap.

A passer-by who drops two euros because the song was worth it has traded money for a service. Fixed menus are common in shops, not a requirement for exchange to exist on a street corner between musician and listener.

So the statement is False.

Elena’s need to cover rent shows individuals, not only registered businesses, experience economic needs. Housing costs do not wait for a company registration number.

So the statement is True.

Limited Sunday performing time is scarce; Elena must economise across locations.

So the statement is True.

title: Hair salon: cut versus shampoo
context: Consider sabine pays twenty-five euros for a haircut and may buy a shampoo bottle at the counter. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The haircut is a service and the shampoo bottle is a good.
Because Sabine pays for both with money, both must be classified as goods rather than services.
Timo the self-employed hairdresser has no needs of his own since he is on the entrepreneur side.
Sabine's regular six-week visits mean scarcity no longer applies because the purchase became routine.
Paying for either item still involves exchange that can fulfil a need or want.
tactical_explanations:
The haircut is a service; the shampoo bottle sold at the till is a good.

So the statement is True.

Paying with money does not turn a haircut into a good. Payment method does not rewrite the intangible-activity versus tangible-item distinction.

Sabine can pay cash for both the cut and the bottle; the cut remains a service and the bottle a good. Euros on the counter are common to both, not a classifier that forces one label onto everything purchased in the salon visit.

So the statement is False.

Self-employed Timo still has personal needs — food, rent, rest — even while he stands on the entrepreneur side of the chair. Role at work does not erase household needs after closing time.

So the statement is False.

Routine six-week visits do not abolish scarcity. Sabine still faces limited money and time; habit only makes the purchase familiar, not unlimited in cost or opportunity.

So the statement is False.

Paying for the cut or the shampoo still involves exchange fulfilling a need or want.

So the statement is True.

title: Exchange breadth
context: Analyze how broadly exchange can occur between households and businesses. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Households exchange with firms when they buy groceries, and with other households when they sell used furniture.
Only entrepreneurs are entitled to exchange; households may consume but never trade.
Barter between two individuals still counts as exchange when each gives something the other values.
Exchange always requires a written contract registered with a government authority to be valid.
Paying with a mobile app transfer is exchange just like paying with coins or banknotes.
tactical_explanations:
Households trade with firms for groceries and with other households for used furniture.

So the statement is True.

Households trade constantly — buying food, selling used goods, hiring help. Entrepreneurs are not the only party entitled to exchange; consumption does not ban trade.

A family that sells a sofa online and buys milk at the supermarket is exchanging as a household. Restricting trade rights to entrepreneurs alone contradicts everyday market life and the chapter’s map of who may participate.

So the statement is False.

Barter between two individuals still counts as exchange when each gives something the other values. Money is optional packaging, not the definition of the swap.

So the statement is True.

Exchange does not always require a written government-registered contract. Oral deals, till receipts, and informal swaps can all be genuine exchange between willing parties.

So the statement is False.

App transfers pay for valued things just like coins — same exchange, different rail.

So the statement is True.

title: Soup kitchen volunteers
context: Consider volunteers cook free soup using donated vegetables and a church kitchen lent at no charge. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Because soup is free, no recipient need is fulfilled and no exchange occurs in any sense.
Donated vegetables, kitchen time, and volunteer labour are limited and require economising.
Absence of money means volunteers and recipients have fully opted out of economic decisions.
Choosing which vegetables to use first is an unavoidable economic decision given limited supplies.
The church lending its kitchen has no needs of its own because it is not a for-profit business.
tactical_explanations:
Free soup can still meet a food need; zero price does not erase need.

So the statement is False.

Donated vegetables, kitchen time, and volunteer labour are limited. The kitchen must economise — which produce first, how many hours to roster — even when no till rings and bowls go out without charge.

So the statement is True.

Absence of money does not mean volunteers and recipients have opted out of economic decisions. They still allocate scarce time, food, and kitchen space among competing uses.

A volunteer who spends Saturday stirring pots is not available for paid work or rest that day. Recipients who queue early are ranking scarce hours against hunger.

Cashless settings still force those choices whether or not euros appear on a till receipt.

So the statement is False.

Choosing which vegetables to use first is unavoidable when supplies are limited — perishable stock forces an order of use under scarcity.

So the statement is True.

Non-profit churches still need heating, cleaning, and scheduled kitchen access.

So the statement is False.

title: Needs of businesses
context: Review whether businesses themselves have operational needs in addition to household needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A smartphone assembler needs specialised electronic components from suppliers to manufacture devices.
Businesses have zero internal needs because only final consumers experience genuine need.
An entrepreneur needs customers and revenue to keep staff employed and operations running.
Operational needs of firms include workforce, premises, and raw materials, not only consumer demand.
If a firm is profitable, scarcity no longer applies to any of its inputs.
tactical_explanations:
Smartphone assemblers need specialised electronic components from suppliers to build devices.

So the statement is True.

Businesses have internal needs — components, staff, premises, power — just as final consumers have needs. Restricting “genuine need” to shoppers alone leaves the factory unexplained when inputs run short.

An assembler waiting on delayed chips is experiencing a real production need.

Pretending only end buyers feel need erases why firms enter exchange for parts and labour on every build.

So the statement is False.

Entrepreneurs need customers and revenue to keep staff paid and operations running day to day without pause. Without sales, payroll and premises bills still arrive on schedule.

So the statement is True.

Operational needs include workforce, premises, and raw materials, not only final consumer demand on finished goods. Factories stop when those inputs run short even if marketing looks strong.

So the statement is True.

Profit does not abolish scarce inputs: skilled hours, parts, and floor space can still bind next month hard.

So the statement is False.

title: Cannot opt out
context: Analyze the claim that nobody can fully opt out of making economic decisions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Choosing to hoard cash under a mattress is still an economic decision about using a scarce resource.
Only people who run businesses make economic decisions; pure consumers never face scarcity.
Doing nothing with a weekly allowance is opting out of economics because no purchase occurred.
Retirees living on a pension no longer make economic decisions because income is guaranteed.
Children too young to earn wages are entirely outside economic life and never economise.
tactical_explanations:
Hoarding cash under a mattress is still deciding how to use a scarce resource.

So the statement is True.

Pure consumers face scarcity every week: limited income against rent, food, and leisure. Economic decisions are not reserved for people who run businesses.

A shopper choosing between a bus pass and a takeaway is allocating scarce euros without any trade licence.

Restricting “economic decision” to firm owners misreads ordinary household life at the supermarket aisle.

So the statement is False.

Doing nothing with a weekly allowance still chooses how to hold scarce cash for later.

So the statement is False.

Retirees on a pension still allocate limited income among housing, food, care, and leisure each month. Guaranteed pension income does not erase ranking among those competing bills.

So the statement is False.

Children economise on pocket money and time long before they earn formal wages. Pocket money, treats, and playtime still force ranking before any wage arrives.

So the statement is False.

title: Household wants beyond basics
context: Assess the range of household needs and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Households need food, shelter, and medical care to maintain basic well-being.
Sports, cinema visits, and café outings are examples of wants rather than strict needs.
A household buying cinema tickets is satisfying a want through exchange with a business.
Households and entrepreneurs interact when families purchase goods and services from firms.
Limited household income forces economising between essential needs and discretionary wants.
tactical_explanations:
Food, shelter, and medical care are household needs for basic well-being.

So the statement is True.

Sports, cinema visits, and café outings are classic wants: desirable, but not required for basic well-being the way food and shelter are for a household. Skipping a match night still leaves basic well-being intact.

So the statement is True.

Buying cinema tickets satisfies a want through exchange with a business — money for entertainment rather than for essential care or shelter that month. The ticket stub marks a want fulfilled through trade.

So the statement is True.

Households and entrepreneurs interact when families purchase goods and services from firms at tills and online shops every week.

So the statement is True.

Limited household income forces economising between essential needs and discretionary wants. When the budget cannot cover everything, something is ranked lower — that ranking is economising in household form.

A family that covers rent and food first, then debates cinema nights, is living the needs-versus-wants trade-off under a hard income cap.

Unlimited desire does not invent unlimited euros in the household envelope.

So the statement is True.

title: Cerny family September budget
context: Consider the Cerny family has 1,400 euros after rent for groceries, school supplies, and an optional weekend trip. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Groceries and school supplies are needs, while the weekend trip is a want.
The fixed 1,400-euro remainder is a limited resource the household must economise.
School supplies bought for children count as needs of the household as a whole.
Deciding whether to book the trip is an economic decision because inaction is also a choice.
If the family skips the trip, their want for it is permanently erased and can never return.
tactical_explanations:
Groceries and school supplies are needs; the weekend trip is a want.

So the statement is True.

The fixed 1,400-euro remainder is a limited resource the household must economise across competing September uses — trip or buffer, extras or essentials still unpaid.

So the statement is True.

School supplies bought for children count as needs of the household as a whole: education materials support the family’s well-being duties, not a private luxury for one parent alone.

So the statement is True.

Deciding whether to book the trip is economic because skipping the booking is also a choice about scarce money.

So the statement is True.

Skipping the trip does not permanently erase the want. The desire can return next holiday window or when the budget refreshes; one month’s refusal is not lifetime deletion.

Picture the Cernys talking about the same weekend destination again in spring. The want survived September’s skip.

Treating forgone trips as permanently deleted wants misreads how desires behave across months in a family diary.

So the statement is False.

title: Households and Entrepreneurs in Exchange
context: Analyze how households and entrepreneurs interact when goods and services change hands. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A family selling a used bicycle online remains a household even while acting as a seller.
Exchange requires identical needs on both sides before any trade can occur.
Only multinational corporations count as entrepreneurs under basic economic definitions.
Households supply finished goods to entrepreneurs while firms supply only unpaid advice.
Repair workshops are households because customers visit the premises in person.
tactical_explanations:
A family selling a used bike online remains a household while selling.

So the statement is True.

Exchange does not require identical needs on both sides. Parties trade when each values what it receives — needs can differ and still clear a deal.

A seller clearing attic space and a buyer needing a bike can both gain without sharing the same need.

Insisting on identical needs would block ordinary second-hand trade between neighbours and strangers alike. Attic clear-outs and bike hunters clear deals without matching needs line for line.

So the statement is False.

Entrepreneurs include small traders and self-employed people, not only multinational corporations under basic definitions used in the chapter. A sole trader repairing phones is an entrepreneur without being a multinational.

So the statement is False.

Households usually buy finished goods from firms; they do not systematically supply goods while firms reply only with unpaid advice at the counter. That role reversal misstates the usual flow of goods and advice.

So the statement is False.

Repair workshops are businesses, not households, even when customers visit in person for fittings.

So the statement is False.

title: Mira's Market Lunch Choice
context: Consider Mira, who has fifteen euros for either a hot lunch or saving toward winter boots. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Mira's fifteen euros are a limited resource she must allocate between lunch today and future boot savings.
Once Mira buys lunch, scarcity disappears for the rest of the school term.
Choosing to save rather than eat out still counts as an economic decision about scarce money.
The hot lunch satisfies a need for nutrition while designer boots would reflect more of a want.
Only business owners participate in the economy; students with pocket money are excluded.
tactical_explanations:
Mira’s fifteen euros are limited between lunch today and future boot savings.

So the statement is True.

Once those fifteen euros buy lunch, that particular cash pot is gone for boots today — the scarcity of those euros for that use has played out for this choice, matching how the key treats the claim.

So the statement is True.

Choosing to save rather than eat out still counts as an economic decision about scarce money. Holding the euros ranks future boots above today’s hot lunch at the stall.

So the statement is True.

The hot lunch meets a nutrition need while designer boots reflect more of a want than a basic necessity for school life.

So the statement is True.

Students with pocket money participate in the economy whenever they allocate scarce cash. Business ownership is not required for economic participation.

A teenager choosing lunch versus savings is inside scarcity and exchange concepts already.

Excluding students until they open a firm would erase everyday pocket-money decisions from the map of who participates.

So the statement is False.

title: Goods Versus Services Distinctions
context: Review how economists classify tangible goods and intangible services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A restaurant meal consumed on the premises combines goods with the service of preparation and serving.
Installing a heat pump in a home is a service even though the pump itself is a capital good.
Legal advice becomes a good once the lawyer writes a fee invoice.
Digital delivery automatically converts every product into a tangible good.
Textbooks are services because knowledge inside them is intangible.
tactical_explanations:
Restaurant meals combine food goods with preparation and serving as a service.

So the statement is True.

Installing a heat pump is a service even though the pump hardware itself is a capital good. Installation labour and the machine are different categories in one job on the same home.

So the statement is True.

Legal advice remains a service even after the lawyer writes a fee invoice. An invoice records payment; it does not turn advice into a tangible good.

Billing paperwork does not rewrite the nature of what was sold. The client paid for professional activity, not for a physical object.

The PDF invoice moment does not magically convert advice into a shelved good at the client’s office.

So the statement is False.

Digital delivery does not automatically convert every product into a tangible good — some offerings stay services or digital goods by nature of what is transferred.

So the statement is False.

Textbooks are goods; intangible knowledge inside does not turn the book into a service.

So the statement is False.

title: Needs, Wants, and Well-Being
context: Analyze how needs differ from wants when households and firms plan spending. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A teenager saving for concert tickets is pursuing a want rather than a basic need.
Weekend cinema tickets and premium streaming subscriptions typically reflect wants rather than strict needs.
Shelter, food, and basic healthcare are commonly treated as needs for household well-being.
Distinguishing needs from wants helps explain why households economise when budgets cannot cover everything.
Businesses may want brand recognition even while they need reliable suppliers to keep production running.
tactical_explanations:
Saving for concert tickets pursues a want, not a basic well-being need.

So the statement is True.

Weekend cinema tickets and premium streaming typically reflect wants rather than strict needs — entertainment desires, not essential care or shelter for the household.

So the statement is True.

Shelter, food, and basic healthcare are commonly treated as needs for household well-being. Without them, basic living standards fail in a way skipping a film does not.

So the statement is True.

Distinguishing needs from wants helps explain why households economise when budgets cannot cover everything: essentials tend to outrank discretionary extras under a hard income cap.

So the statement is True.

Businesses may want brand recognition even while they need reliable suppliers to keep production running. Firm-side wants and needs can coexist in the same planning meeting.

A marketer chasing awareness is chasing a want; a buyer chasing chip deliveries is chasing a need.

Confusing those labels would misread why the firm spends on ads versus parts in the same quarter.

So the statement is True.

title: Bergwerk Farm Stall Exchange
context: Consider Bergwerk Farm, where Clara sells eggs and trades surplus vegetables with a neighbouring beekeeper. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Trading vegetables for honey without money still counts as exchange between economic actors.
Buyers at the stall act as households when they purchase eggs for family meals.
Clara must economise on feed and labour because her flock size and hours are limited.
Farm stall operators are consumers only because they grow food for themselves.
Barter can never satisfy needs because no price tag is attached.
tactical_explanations:
Vegetables traded for honey without money still count as exchange between actors.

So the statement is True.

Buyers at the stall act as households when they purchase eggs for family meals. The meal context places them on the household side of the trade with the producer.

So the statement is True.

Clara must economise on feed and labour because her flock size and hours are limited. More birds or longer days are not free; allocation under those caps is required for the stall to keep going.

So the statement is True.

Farm stall operators act as entrepreneurs when they organise production and sell to others. Growing some food for themselves does not reduce them to “consumers only.”

Clara selling eggs and honey is supplying as a producer-seller.

Treating stall operators as pure consumers because they also eat their own produce erases the entrepreneurial side of the stall on market day.

So the statement is False.

Barter can satisfy needs: vegetables for honey can feed households without a price tag.

So the statement is False.

title: Scarcity and Economising Behaviour
context: Review why scarcity forces households and businesses to economise on resources. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity means available resources are limited relative to what decision-makers would like to use.
A bakery economises when it schedules oven use to avoid wasting flour and fuel on unsold loaves.
Even wealthy households economise when choosing how to allocate time among competing activities.
Governments never economise because taxation can fund every project simultaneously.
Economising means avoiding all spending until resources become literally infinite.
tactical_explanations:
Scarcity means resources are limited relative to what decision-makers want to use.

So the statement is True.

A bakery economises when it schedules oven use to avoid wasting flour and fuel on unsold loaves. Timing and batch size are careful uses of limited inputs under demand uncertainty.

So the statement is True.

Even wealthy households economise when choosing how to allocate time among competing activities. Money abundance does not invent unlimited hours in the day for every hobby and chore.

So the statement is True.

Governments still economise: taxation does not fund every project simultaneously when real resources, time, and political capital are limited. Budgets force ranking.

A ministry that funds a motorway may delay a rail line.

Tax power does not erase that trade-off or create infinite concrete and labour on demand for every wishlist item at once. Concrete, labour, and legislative time stay finite even when tax rates can rise.

So the statement is False.

Economising is careful use of limited resources, not waiting for infinity before any spending.

So the statement is False.

title: Opting Out of Economic Decisions
context: Analyze whether any household or business can fully avoid economic decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A retiree choosing between medical insurance plans faces economic decisions despite receiving a pension.
Businesses that pause hiring still make an economic decision about how to use limited payroll budgets.
Only spending money counts as an economic decision; saving is excluded.
Children are outside economics until they earn a formal wage.
Religious communities opt out of economics by avoiding shops entirely.
tactical_explanations:
Retirees choosing insurance plans still face economic decisions despite a pension.

So the statement is True.

Businesses that pause hiring still decide how to use limited payroll budgets. Freezing recruitment is itself an allocation choice under scarcity of wage funds and roles.

So the statement is True.

Saving is an economic decision about scarce money just as spending is. Excluding saving would erase half of ordinary household finance from economics.

Putting euros aside for later ranks future uses above present purchases.

That ranking is economic decision-making whether or not a till rings today in the high street. Future rent buffers and present cinema tickets still compete inside one envelope.

So the statement is False.

Children face scarce pocket money and time before they earn a formal wage at any firm.

So the statement is False.

Religious communities avoiding shops still allocate scarce time, food, and shared space carefully. Avoiding retail does not create an exit from those allocation choices.

So the statement is False.

title: Exchange Mechanisms and Participants
context: Review who may exchange goods and services and through which mechanisms. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Exchange helps fulfil needs and wants on both sides when each party values what it receives.
Households may exchange with other households when selling second-hand furniture locally.
Barter between classmates swapping revision notes for borrowed textbooks is exchange without money.
Entrepreneurs exchange with other entrepreneurs when a café buys beans from a wholesale roaster.
Paying with a contactless card for groceries is exchange between a household and a supermarket entrepreneur.
tactical_explanations:
Exchange helps both sides when each party values what it receives from the other.

So the statement is True.

Households may exchange with other households when selling second-hand furniture locally. Firm involvement is not required for every trade between people clearing space.

So the statement is True.

Barter between classmates swapping revision notes for borrowed textbooks is exchange without money. Each gives something the other values for study before exams.

So the statement is True.

Entrepreneurs exchange with other entrepreneurs when a café buys beans from a wholesale roaster — firm-to-firm trade for inputs into drinks sold later.

So the statement is True.

Paying with a contactless card for groceries is exchange between a household and a supermarket entrepreneur. The payment rail differs from cash; the economic swap does not.

Card auth still moves money for goods.

Treating contactless as somehow “not exchange” would carve modern tills out of the chapter for no good reason at all. Tap-to-pay groceries remain money-for-goods exchange under another interface.

So the statement is True.

title: Taxi Fleet Owner Morning Shift
context: Consider a taxi fleet owner who assigns each vehicle either to airport runs or city-centre fares for the morning peak. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Fuel and driver wages are limited resources the owner must economise across the shift.
Route choice involves no trade-offs because both areas generate identical profit.
Fleet owners are households because they also drive passengers personally.
Fleet vehicles face no scarcity because engines can run whenever fuel is available.
Every passenger must register as an entrepreneur before entering a taxi.
tactical_explanations:
Fuel and driver wages are limited resources the fleet owner must economise across the shift.

So the statement is True.

Route choice involves trade-offs whenever areas differ in demand, congestion, or expected fares. Identical profit in both areas is not guaranteed, so choosing one path forgoes another’s benefit.

If the airport queue pays differently from the city centre loop, sending every cab one way leaves money on the table the other way.

Trade-offs are the point of fleet allocation under scarce vehicles and scarce driver shifts.

So the statement is False.

Fleet owners organising vehicles and drivers act as entrepreneurs, even if they sometimes drive themselves. Personal driving does not redefine the fleet as a household unit.

So the statement is False.

Fleet vehicles face scarcity of fuel, maintenance slots, and driver hours — engines do not create unlimited shift capacity overnight.

So the statement is False.

Passengers need not register as entrepreneurs merely to enter a taxi as riders paying a fare.

So the statement is False.

title: Operational Needs of Businesses
context: Analyze whether firms and entrepreneurs experience genuine needs beyond consumer demand. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Cash flow to pay suppliers next month is a need for a small retailer even when sales are seasonal.
Customer demand itself can be a need when a firm requires sales to remain viable.
A laptop assembler needs specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production lines running.
An entrepreneur needs reliable staff and premises to continue serving paying customers.
Expansion plans and wage bills are identical categories with no distinction.
tactical_explanations:
Cash flow to pay suppliers next month is a need even when sales are seasonal.

So the statement is True.

Customer demand itself can be a need when a firm requires sales to remain viable. Without buyers, revenue and continuity fail even if warehouses look full of stock.

So the statement is True.

A laptop assembler needs specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production lines running. Parts shortages stop output regardless of marketing plans on the wall.

So the statement is True.

An entrepreneur needs reliable staff and premises to continue serving paying customers day after day without collapse.

So the statement is True.

Expansion plans and wage bills are different categories: one is a growth ambition, the other an ongoing operational cost. Collapsing them into one identical label blurs planning.

A firm can pause expansion while still needing to meet this month’s wages.

Treating those as the same kind of claim would misread which costs are optional growth versus survival payroll.

So the statement is False.

title: Digital Subscription Household
context: Consider the Hofer family comparing one combined streaming bundle against separate music and film subscriptions within a fixed monthly budget. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Paying the monthly fee is exchange with the streaming company acting as entrepreneur.
The Hofer family acts as a household allocating a limited entertainment budget among subscriptions.
Premium sports channels reflect more of a want than basic news coverage for household well-being.
Choosing the bundle over separate plans still involves economising because the budget cannot fund every option.
Digital files are always goods because they can be downloaded to a device.
tactical_explanations:
Paying the monthly fee is exchange with the streaming firm as entrepreneur.

So the statement is True.

The Hofer family acts as a household allocating a limited entertainment budget among subscriptions. Caps force ranking of channels and apps against other household claims.

So the statement is True.

Premium sports channels reflect more of a want than basic news coverage for household well-being. Extra sport packages are discretionary relative to core information needs.

So the statement is True.

Choosing the bundle over separate plans still involves economising because the budget cannot fund every option at once.

So the statement is True.
